body:
I found it weird that 1 row would match (expected 2) so did some more digging.

I found that in python 3.12 both children would get UPDATEs with the same new updated_at timestamp
```diff
UPDATE child SET created_by_id=?, updated_at=? WHERE child.id = ? AND child.updated_at = ?
+[(None, '2025-07-23 10:55:19.927921', 1, '2025-07-23 10:55:19.923921'), (None, '2025-07-23 10:55:19.927921', 2, '2025-07-23 10:55:19.923921')]
DELETE FROM child WHERE child.id = ? AND child.updated_at = ?
+[(1, '2025-07-23 10:55:19.927921'), (2, '2025-07-23 10:55:19.927921')]
DELETE FROM parent WHERE parent.id = ?
(1,)
COMMIT
```

In python 3.13, they get slightly different timestamps in the UPDATE statement, however the first (new) timestamp is used in the DELETE statement

```diff
UPDATE child SET created_by_id=?, updated_at=? WHERE child.id = ? AND child.updated_at = ?
-[(None, '2025-07-23 11:31:24.168741', 1, '2025-07-23 11:31:24.164506'), (None, '2025-07-23 11:31:24.168748', 2, '2025-07-23 11:31:24.164512')]
DELETE FROM child WHERE child.id = ? AND child.updated_at = ?
-[(1, '2025-07-23 11:31:24.168741'), (2, '2025-07-23 11:31:24.168741')]
ROLLBACK
```

Am away this week can potentially look later in week or next week

hi -

~~I think the version counter being used here is not appropriate, because it is generating a "random" version and things are then not matching up as expected.  in particular the issue seems to be when the version id counter is given the current version and asked to produce the "next" version, it produces a different value each time, and this is not expected by the ORM.~~ this is incorrect    ~~I can reproduce the error on older pythons as well and you might find that python 3.12 might reproduce if you set PYTHONHASHSEED=random.~~ incorrect

If i use the following version routine that's guaranteed to produce the same "subsequent" version given the "previous" version, there's no issue (**edit** because it covers up the bug for a different reason):

```py
next_version = {}

def dt(version):
    if version not in next_version:
        next_version[version] = datetime.now()

    return next_version[version]

```

~~strategies like removing the microseconds portion of the date will "work" as well but not consistently, the main thing is that previous version is being given and the new version has to be deterministic from that number.~~

I can look in a few days more deeply to review the nature of this behavior.
~~this is expected behavior, the versions need to be in a sequence that is at least as predictable as the previous version id~~ incorrect

Thanks for digging into this. That makes sense and seems like reasonable workaround. 

Are the docs incorrect though?

https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/versioning.html gives an example which also disregards the previous version.
```python
__mapper_args__ = {
        "version_id_col": version_uuid,
        "version_id_generator": lambda version: uuid.uuid4().hex,
    }
```

> The persistence engine will call upon uuid.uuid4() each time a User object is subject to an INSERT or an UPDATE. In this case, our version generation function can disregard the incoming value of version, as the uuid4() function generates identifiers without any prerequisite value. If we were using a sequential versioning scheme such as numeric or a special character system, we could make use of the given version in order to help determine the subsequent value.

it seems like they are! reopening as a docs bug.

it seems like we would need to implement a similar implementation, but a simple dict like mike did in the example is not great since that's a memory leak waiting to happen :(

not sure how to best showcase this

Thanks,

I also can't figure out a way to ensure the new version_id is unique per object. 

For example, if 2 User objects were created at the same time (same initial version_id), and ObjectA gets updated, this will generate the "next" version in the sequence, and whenever ObjectB is updated, it will receive this same version_id.
In my case of using datetime or if you wanted a UUID as in the doc example, this would not work.
version should be unique per object, so that's fine if you have the same version in more than one user in your case. that's the same with a plain numeric version, every object will start at version 1

~~sure the doc version is not ideal either~~ it's fine

I think this problem is only happening here because it's using post_update, though.    **DING** I never went back and checked to understand the complete codepath by which it needs to get the same version identifier twice from the function

> version should be unique per object, so that's fine if you have the same version in more than one user in your case. that's the same with a plain numeric version, every object will start at version 1

Yeah, I get that normally you could have multiple objects with version =1,

However in my case, where I want to use the "updated at" timestamp as my version, the following would happen:

```python
item1 = Item()
item2 = Item()
session.add(item1)
session.add(item2)
session.commit()
item1.updated_at
# datetime.datetime(2025, 8, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0)
item2.updated_at
# datetime.datetime(2025, 8, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0)

#....some time later
item1.some_prop = value
session.commit()

item1.updated_at
# datetime.datetime(2025, 8, 5, 0, 0, 1, 0)

#....a day later
item2.some_prop = value
session.commit()

item2.updated_at
# datetime.datetime(2025, 8, 5, 0, 0, 1, 0)


item1.updated_at == item2.updated_at
# True
```
here, item2's "version" is updated to the "next in sequence" which was dictated by whenever item1 happened to be updated

The same thing would happen using UUID's, you wouldn't actually get a unique id for item2's version. Sure this doesn't cause a database conflict, but it can easily be an issue at the application level depending on your requirements
understood. yes, that wouldn't be optimal.

rename.from: post_update causes cascaded DELETE statement to fail
rename.to: post_update does not apply state to updated objects in a multi-execute correctly

body: The bug is that more than one row is received in post_update and the ORM is applying the version id from the first object to the second object, so that they both have the same version id, but with this particular versioning scheme, the two objects have different versions this is the fix ```diff diff --git a/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/persistence.py b/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/persistence.py index 1d6b4abf6..4b0a008ba 100644 --- a/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/persistence.py +++ b/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/persistence.py @@ -1379,7 +1379,7 @@ def _emit_post_update_statements( ) rows += c.rowcount - for state, state_dict, mapper_rec, connection, params in records: + for i, (state, state_dict, mapper_rec, connection, params) in enumerate(records): _postfetch_post_update( mapper_rec, uowtransaction, @@ -1387,7 +1387,7 @@ def _emit_post_update_statements( state, state_dict, c, - c.context.compiled_parameters[0], + c.context.compiled_parameters[i], ) if check_rowcount:

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**apply correct pre-fetch params to post updated rows** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/6065
